title: Athaliah's Coup and the Hidden King
summary: When her son Ahaziah is killed, Athaliah, Ahab's daughter, sets out to destroy the whole royal family of Judah and rules in Jerusalem for six years. But Ahaziah's sister Jehosheba hides his infant son Joash in the temple. In the seventh year the priest Jehoiada organizes the royal guard, crowns the boy in the temple, and has Athaliah executed; he renews the covenant between the LORD, the king, and the people, and the temple of Baal in Jerusalem is torn down.
story: The alliance between Judah and the house of Ahab, begun under Jehoshaphat (1 Kings 22:44) and sealed by marriage (8:18), now nearly destroys the line of David. While Jehu wipes out Ahab's house in the north (chapters 9 and 10), Ahab's daughter seizes power in the south and tries to wipe out David's house. This is one of the Bible's moments of greatest danger for the promise God made to David, that his house and throne would endure (2 Samuel 7:16) and that he would have a lamp in Jerusalem (8:19). The promise survives in a single infant, hidden in God's house. The next chapter follows the reign of the boy who was rescued.
historical:
Athaliah reigned about 841 to 835 BC, the only person not of David's line to rule Judah in the whole history of the kingdom, and the only reigning queen in Israel or Judah. She was the daughter of Ahab (8:18) and granddaughter of Omri (8:26), and she brought the worship of Baal to Jerusalem as her mother Jezebel had brought it to Samaria. There was a temple of Baal in Jerusalem, with its own priest, Mattan (verse 18). The Chronicler's parallel account (2 Chronicles 22:10-23:21) adds that Jehosheba was the wife of Jehoiada the priest, which explains how the child could be hidden in the temple precincts, and it gives a larger role to the Levites in the coup.

The Carites (verses 4 and 19) are usually understood as foreign mercenaries serving as a royal bodyguard, perhaps from Caria in southwestern Asia Minor, a region known for supplying mercenaries; some connect them with the Cherethites who served as David's bodyguard (2 Samuel 8:18). Joash (also spelled Jehoash) became king around 835 BC at the age of seven.
cultural:
Killing a rival's heirs was a standard way to secure a usurped throne, as Jehu had just done in the north. Athaliah's attempt to destroy all the royal offspring was a bid to end the dynasty entirely and rule in her own right. A royal infant would have had a wet nurse, who was hidden with him. The temple, with its storerooms and chambers, was one of the few places in Jerusalem where a child could be kept out of the palace's sight, especially under the protection of the priesthood.

The coronation ritual in verse 12 has several elements. The crown marked royal authority. The Testimony (edut) was likely a written document of the covenant, perhaps a copy of the law that Deuteronomy 17:18-19 says a king should keep and read, or a royal charter; interpreters are not certain. Anointing with oil set the king apart, and the people's acclaim, Long live the king, confirmed him publicly. The king stood by the pillar according to custom (verse 14), a fixed place in the temple court for royal ceremonies (compare Josiah in 23:3). The guard changes on the Sabbath (verses 5-9) allowed Jehoiada to have twice the usual number of soldiers present at once without raising suspicion.
literary: The chapter moves from death to life, from hiding to revelation, and from usurpation to covenant. Its opening verses are brief and chilling: Athaliah saw that her son was dead and set out to destroy all the royal seed. The counter-move is just as brief: Jehosheba took Joash and stole him away. The seven-year structure (six years hidden, the coup in the seventh) gives a sense of completion. Jehoiada's detailed instructions to the guards slow the pace and build tension, and the coronation scene erupts with noise: trumpets, clapping, and the cry of the people. Athaliah's cry, “Treason! Treason!” (verse 14), is bitterly ironic, since her own reign began with treason and murder. The chapter ends with two covenants (verse 17), the destruction of Baal's temple (18), and a quiet city (20), in pointed contrast to the bloodshed of Jehu's reform in the chapter before.

outline.t: Athaliah destroys the royal family; Joash is hidden
Jehoiada's plan and the coronation of Joash
Covenant renewal, Baal's temple destroyed, and Joash enthroned

doctrines.note: Jehoiada makes a covenant between the LORD and the king and the people that they would be the LORD's people (verse 17). Restoring the king of David's line goes with renewing the whole nation's covenant with God.
God's promise to David hangs on one hidden infant, rescued by a courageous woman and protected by a priest. God keeps his word through ordinary people's risky faithfulness, often out of sight.
The chapter asks who has the right to rule God's people. Athaliah held power for six years, but the rightful king was hidden in God's house, waiting to be revealed.

words.note: Berit, covenant, a binding agreement with obligations and oaths. Jehoiada first makes a berit with the guard commanders to secure their loyalty (verse 4), then a berit between the LORD, the king, and the people, and another between the king and the people (verse 17). The word ties Joash's accession to Israel's covenant identity.

Edut, testimony, used of the tablets of the law in the ark (the ark of the testimony) and of God's decrees. Jehoiada gives the young king the edut at his coronation (verse 12). Whatever the exact document, it signals that the king rules under God's law, not above it.

Zera, seed or offspring. Athaliah sets out to destroy all the royal zera (verse 1). The word is central to the Bible's promises: the seed of the woman (Genesis 3:15), the seed of Abraham, and the seed of David whose throne God would establish (2 Samuel 7:12). Here that seed is reduced to one child.

christ: This chapter is a vivid instance of a pattern that runs through the Bible: the promised line threatened with extinction and preserved by God. The New Testament genealogy of Jesus runs through this very line of David's kings (Matthew 1:6-11; Matthew passes over Joash and two other kings by name, but the line runs through him), and it would not exist if Jehosheba had not rescued Joash. The pattern recurs at Jesus' birth. As Athaliah tried to kill the royal heirs, Herod ordered the killing of the boys of Bethlehem to eliminate a newborn king, and the child was hidden in Egypt until the danger passed (Matthew 2:13-18). These are thematic parallels rather than predictions, but they show how seriously the Bible takes God's promise to give David a son who would reign forever, a promise the New Testament sees kept in Jesus (Luke 1:32-33).
questions: Jehosheba risked her life to hide a child and preserve David's line. What does her courage suggest about the role of ordinary people in keeping God's purposes alive?
For six years the rightful king was hidden while a usurper ruled. How does this story speak to times when evil seems to be in charge and God's purposes seem hidden?
Jehoiada's reform began with a covenant to be the LORD's people. What is the difference between changing leaders and renewing a people's commitment to God?
